title: The Secular Guarantee of Maintenance Against Destitution
hook: A landmark constitutional ruling established that statutory maintenance protections against vagrancy apply universally across personal laws.
summary:
When an elderly woman was divorced by irrevocable pronouncement after more than four decades of marriage, she sought a monthly maintenance allowance to prevent complete destitution. The former spouse resisted the claim, arguing that his obligations under personal law terminated upon the expiration of the customary post-divorce waiting period and the return of the agreed marriage settlement.

The Supreme Court affirmed that the statutory maintenance regime under criminal procedure operates as a secular, public measure designed to eradicate vagrancy and economic abandonment. The bench ruled that statutory definitions extending protection to divorced women who remain unmarried supersede any conflicting obligations under personal religious codes.

Addressing the interaction between statutory maintenance and customary marital payments, the court determined that marriage consideration paid at the time of marriage does not constitute an amount payable on divorce under statutory exemptions. Consequently, the former husband remained under an enforceable obligation to provide maintenance so long as the divorced spouse lacked the independent means to maintain herself.

social.hook: Divorced after 43 years of marriage, an elderly woman asked a court for monthly survival maintenance.
social.script: Divorced after 43 years of marriage, an elderly woman asked a court for monthly survival maintenance. With no income, she applied under Section 125 of the criminal procedure code. Her former husband pronounced an irrevocable divorce, deposited three thousand rupees as marriage dower, and argued that personal law ended his financial duty after the three month waiting period. In 1985, a five judge Constitution Bench unanimously dismissed his appeal. The Supreme Court held that Section 125 is a secular safeguard against destitution applying to every citizen regardless of religion, and marriage dower is not a sum payable on divorce. You be the judge. Full case notes are on the Courtroom Chronicles website.

carousel.text: Divorced after 43 years of marriage, an elderly woman asked a court for monthly survival maintenance.

carousel.heading: What happened
carousel.text: Her former spouse deposited her marriage dower and claimed his maintenance obligation ended after the customary post-divorce waiting period.

carousel.heading: The legal question
carousel.text: Does the secular maintenance remedy under criminal procedure override personal law defenses when a divorced woman faces destitution?

carousel.heading: The ruling
carousel.text: The Supreme Court unanimously held that statutory maintenance applies universally across all communities and marriage dower is not a divorce payment.

carousel.heading: Why it matters
carousel.text: The ruling affirmed that preventing vagrancy and economic abandonment is an enforceable secular duty owed to society.
